item.research_question: How does the addition of Vanadium (V) affect the stacking fault energy (SFE), lattice distortion, deformation mechanisms, and strain-hardening behavior of non-equiatomic CoCrNi medium-entropy alloys?
item.material_system: Non-equiatomic CoCrNiV alloys with compositions Co36Cr36Ni26V2 (2V), Co35Cr35Ni24V6 (6V), and Co33Cr33Ni24V10 (10V)
item.processing_route: Vacuum induction melting of 99.99 wt.% purity raw materials, homogenization at 1473 K for 5 h, water quenching, hot rolling to 1 mm at 1373 K, and annealing at 1473 K for 90 min (2V), 60 min (6V), and 120 min (10V)
item.test_conditions: Room temperature tensile tests at an initial strain rate of 10−3 s−1 using a CMT 5105 testing machine; samples had a gauge length of 10 mm, width of 4 mm, and thickness of 1 mm
key_findings: The 2V alloy exhibits a yield strength of 318 MPa and a uniform elongation of 47%.
The 6V alloy shows a slightly lower yield strength of 307 MPa but higher uniform elongation of 49%.
The 10V alloy demonstrates a dramatic increase in yield strength to 415 MPa with uniform elongation of 42%.
The 2V alloy activates deformation-induced HCP phase transformation, while 6V and 10V alloys remain FCC single-phase after deformation.
The strain-hardening rate of the 6V alloy is lower than that of the 2V alloy at strains below 0.15.
The strain-hardening rate of the 10V alloy is higher than that of the 6V alloy due to severe lattice distortion.
Lattice constants increase monotonously with V enrichment: 2V (a = 0.3563 nm), 6V (a = 0.3576 nm), and 10V (a = 0.3580 nm).
The calculated δ parameters for volume misfit are 1.96% (2V), 2.33% (6V), and 2.61% (10V).
item.mechanism: V addition increases both SFE and lattice distortion; the lower strain-hardening rate of 6V compared to 2V is dominated by the increased SFE which suppresses phase transformation, while the higher strain-hardening rate of 10V compared to 6V is dominated by severe lattice distortion which increases lattice friction stress and facilitates dislocation dissociation into Shockley partials forming SFs.
quotes: The lower strain-hardening rate of 6V alloy than that of 2V alloy is dominated by the SFE.
The higher strain-hardening rate of 10V alloy than that of 6V alloy is dominated by the lattice distortion.
The main deformation mechanisms of CoCrNiV alloy with low V content are dislocation slip, stacking faults, and deformation-induced HCP phase transformation

Question: How does the addition of Vanadium (V) affect the stacking fault energy (SFE), lattice distortion, deformation mechanisms, and strain-hardening behavior of non-equiatomic CoCrNi medium-entropy alloys?. System: Non-equiatomic CoCrNiV alloys with compositions Co36Cr36Ni26V2 (2V), Co35Cr35Ni24V6 (6V), and Co33Cr33Ni24V10 (10V). Processing: Vacuum induction melting of 99.99 wt.% purity raw materials, homogenization at 1473 K for 5 h, water quenching, hot rolling to 1 mm at 1373 K, and annealing at 1473 K for 90 min (2V), 60 min (6V), and 120 min (10V). Test conditions: Room temperature tensile tests at an initial strain rate of 10−3 s−1 using a CMT 5105 testing machine; samples had a gauge length of 10 mm, width of 4 mm, and thickness of 1 mm. Findings: The 2V alloy exhibits a yield strength of 318 MPa and a uniform elongation of 47%.; The 6V alloy shows a slightly lower yield strength of 307 MPa but higher uniform elongation of 49%.; The 10V alloy demonstrates a dramatic increase in yield strength to 415 MPa with uniform elongation of 42%.; The 2V alloy activates deformation-induced HCP phase transformation, while 6V and 10V alloys remain FCC single-phase after deformation.; The strain-hardening rate of the 6V alloy is lower than that of the 2V alloy at strains below 0.15.; The strain-hardening rate of the 10V alloy is higher than that of the 6V alloy due to severe lattice distortion.; Lattice constants increase monotonously with V enrichment: 2V (a = 0.3563 nm), 6V (a = 0.3576 nm), and 10V (a = 0.3580 nm).; The calculated δ parameters for volume misfit are 1.96% (2V), 2.33% (6V), and 2.61% (10V).. Mechanism: V addition increases both SFE and lattice distortion; the lower strain-hardening rate of 6V compared to 2V is dominated by the increased SFE which suppresses phase transformation, while the higher strain-hardening rate of 10V compared to 6V is dominated by severe lattice distortion which increases lattice friction stress and facilitates dislocation dissociation into Shockley partials forming SFs.. Quote: "The lower strain-hardening rate of 6V alloy than that of 2V alloy is dominated by the SFE."
